- [Substack: Andrew Ross Sorkin on the Crash of 1929 & The Parallels We See Today | The Real Eisman Playbook](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/andrew-ross-sorkin-on-the-crash-of-f9e) - 2025-10-27

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Andrew Ross Sorkin discusses the human incentives and policy failures surrounding 1929. Eisman emphasizes leverage, shared institutional exposures, short-selling survival and the danger of assuming officials already understand a crisis. This is mainly historical explanation, not a prediction of another crash. Original Fed records contradict the guest's assertion that policymakers could not contemplate rate increases in 1929, and preexisting bank capital rules qualify the repeated no-rules narrative.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

### 007. There were no genuine regulatory bank-capital requirements before the crash.

**Wrong** | Andrew Ross Sorkin | material factual premise | supporting

[Source at 15:25-16:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yp6EggtUBYI&t=925s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Minimum charter capital and reserve rules already existed. Absence of modern capital-to-asset ratios is not absence of regulatory capital requirements.

Assessment test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.

Further verification: Recheck the original data and subsequent realized outcomes.

- [National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864](https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/national-banking-acts) (2022): National bank rules included minimum capital levels and reserve requirements based on the city's population and designation. These were not modern risk-weighted ratios, but banking was not without capital rules.

## Framework and tools

- Map leverage, shared assets and funding links before calling a downturn systemic.
- Separate correct bearish direction from the ability to survive a short.
- Do not assume policymakers possess all available information or can act promptly.
- Distinguish the crash, the ensuing depression, the start of recovery and full employment.
- Use historical analogies as risk prompts rather than deterministic forecasts.
- Check original policy actions before inferring motives from a narrative.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Margin leverage and equity-loss arithmetic
- 1929 New York Fed discount-rate record
- Bank capital and reserve rules before modern ratios
- Monetary contraction and gold-standard recovery
- Layered leverage in old trusts and modern vehicles

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman interviews Andrew Ross Sorkin. Historical explanations by the guest are kept separate from Eisman's crisis framework and retrospective process revision.
- Opening montage repeats the interview.
- All 1500 caption lines were read.
- Biographical trivia and speculative mental-health characterization are omitted as immaterial to the investment audit.
- Eisman's initial unemployment number is immediately corrected and accepted, so it is not a separate forecast error.
- Book anecdotes remain unresolved where the underlying archives were not inspected.
- Sorkin explicitly says he is not forecasting another 1929.
